s: English population in Canada are lawless crushing the rebellion (many of them, in their methods)

s: Robert Bouchette is a rebel (devoted to liberty and the rights of the people)

s: Robert Bouchette defines rights of the people (as cardinal rights inherent to British subjects)
q: 'When I speak of the rights of the people,' wrote Bouchette, 'I do not mean those abstract or extravagant rights for which some contend, but which are not generally compatible with an organized state of society, but I mean those cardinal rights which are inherent to British subjects, and which, as such, ought not to be denied to the inhabitants of any section of the empire, however remote.'

s: loyalty is a spirit (characterizing loyal Canadians in 1837)
q: fail to be proud of the spirit of loyalty which in 1837 {129} actuated not only persons of British birth, but many faithful sons and daughters of the French-Canadian Church

s: conquest of Canada is a conquest (by British arms during the Seven Years' War)
q: The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.

s: Quebec Act of 1774 grants concessions (by the Quebec Act of the year before)
q: But the conciliatory policy of the successive governors Murray and Carleton, and the concessions granted by the Quebec Act of the year before, had borne {3} fruit

s: Continental Congress sought to induce French Canadians (to join the American revolutionary cause in 1775)
q: When the American colonies broke out in revolution in 1775, the Continental Congress thought to induce the French Canadians to join hands with them.

s: American invasion of Canada (1775) was led by Benedict Arnold
q: when the American leaders Arnold and Montgomery invaded Canada

s: American invasion of Canada (1775) was led by Richard Montgomery

s: French Canadians remained loyal to British rule (the great majority remained at least passively loyal during the invasion)
q: the great majority of the habitants remained at least passively loyal.

s: French Canadians resisted Continental Congress (the mass of the people resisted its appeals)
q: the mass of the people resisted the eloquent appeals of Congress, represented by its emissaries Franklin, Chase, and Carroll

s: Catholic clergy remained loyal to British rule (firmly loyal during the American invasion)
q: The clergy, the seigneurs, and the professional classes--lawyers and physicians and notaries--remained firm in their allegiance to Great Britain

s: Sir Guy Carleton is aided by Colonel Dupre and Captains Dambourges, Dumas, and Marcoux
q: the Canadian officers Colonel Dupre and Captains Dambourges, Dumas, and Marcoux, with many others, were among Carleton's most trusted and efficient aides in driving back the invading Americans.

s: Quebec was defended against American invasion of Canada (1775) (during the siege)
q: at the siege of Quebec by Arnold the Canadian officers Colonel Dupre and Captains Dambourges, Dumas, and Marcoux, with many others, were among Carleton's most trusted and efficient aides in driving back the invading Americans.

s: Frederick Haldimand rules Lower Canada (in the manner of a soldier)
q: But it must be {4} borne in mind that Haldimand ruled the province in the manner of a soldier

s: conquest of Canada placed under British rule (the French inhabitants of Canada were subjected to it)
q: It placed the French inhabitants under the sway of an alien race--a race of another language, of another religion, of other laws, and which differed from them profoundly in temperament and political outlook.

s: Frederick Haldimand considered unreliable Catholic clergy (in 1781, because he believed they had changed their opinions)
q: Sir Frederick Haldimand, then governor of Canada, wrote that although the clergy had been firmly loyal in 1775 and had exerted their powerful influence in favour of Great Britain, they had since then changed their opinions and were no longer to be relied upon.

s: Catholic clergy was led by Mgr Briand (their conduct followed that of the bishop of Quebec)
q: No more devoted subject of Great Britain lived at the time in Lower Canada than Mgr Briand, the bishop of Quebec; and the priests shaped their conduct after that of their superior.

s: French Revolution created a gap between France (and Canada; the gap has not been bridged to this day)
q: That movement created a gap between France and Canada which has not been bridged to this day.

s: War of 1812 is marked by Canada repeatedly invaded by American armies
q: In that war, in which Canada was repeatedly invaded by American armies

s: French-Canadian militiamen fought with English population in Canada (under French-Canadian officers on several battlefields)
q: French-Canadian militiamen under French-Canadian officers fought shoulder to shoulder with their English-speaking fellow-countrymen on several stricken fields of battle

s: Major de Salaberry is won by Major de Salaberry and his French-Canadian soldiers
q: the day was won for British arms by the heroic prowess of Major de Salaberry and his French-Canadian soldiers.

s: Battle of Chateauguay was won by French-Canadian militiamen (for British arms)
q: the day was won for British arms by the heroic prowess of Major de Salaberry and his French-Canadian soldiers.

s: rebellion of 1837 included fighting at St Denis (French-Canadian rebels repulsed British regulars)
q: the fowling-pieces of the French-Canadian rebels had repulsed a force of British regulars at the village of St Denis

s: rebellion of 1837 included skirmishes at St Charles (brisk skirmishes occurred there)
q: brisk skirmishes had taken place at the villages of St Charles and St Eustache.

s: rebellion of 1837 included skirmishes at St Eustache (brisk skirmishes occurred there)
q: brisk skirmishes had taken place at the villages of St Charles and St Eustache.

s: French Canadians dwells with English population in Canada (in peace and amity for a hundred and fifty years)
q: In Canada, however, for a hundred and fifty years French Canadians and English Canadians have, on the whole, dwelt together in peace and amity.

s: English population in Canada dwells with French Canadians (in peace and amity for a hundred and fifty years)
q: In Canada, however, for a hundred and fifty years French Canadians and English Canadians have, on the whole, dwelt together in peace and amity.

s: Canadians has reason to view record of racial peace (whether English or French)
q: The record {2} is one which Canadians, whether they be English or French, have reason to view with satisfaction

s: Canadians is a people of Canada (English or French)
q: The record {2} is one which Canadians, whether they be English or French, have reason to view with satisfaction

s: French Canadians remained in Canada (comparatively few left after the change of rule)
q: Comparatively few Canadians left the country, although they were afforded facilities for so doing.

s: British treats French Canadians (as protected inhabitants rather than a conquered people)
q: The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.

s: French Canadians are Roman Catholics (all French Canadians)
q: All French Canadians were Roman Catholics

s: French-Canadian Church is debarred from House of Commons (Roman Catholics were barred from sitting as members at this time)
q: Roman Catholics were at this time debarred from sitting in the House of Commons at Westminster.

s: Canadian representative Assemblies gives the right of sitting to Catholics of Canada
q: Yet they were given the right of sitting as members in the Canadian representative Assemblies created by the Act of 1791.

s: British government maintains loyalty of French Canadians (during the wars of 1775 and 1812 through conciliatory policy)
q: There can be no doubt that it was the conciliatory policy of the British government which kept the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians loyal to the British crown during the war in 1775 and in 1812.

s: Catholic clergy is loyal to British crown (during the wars of 1775 and 1812)
q: it was the conciliatory policy of the British government which kept the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians loyal to the British crown during the war in 1775 and in 1812.

s: French seigneurs is loyal to British crown (during the wars of 1775 and 1812)
q: it was the conciliatory policy of the British government which kept the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians loyal to the British crown during the war in 1775 and in 1812.

s: French Canadians is loyal to British crown (during the wars of 1775 and 1812)
q: it was the conciliatory policy of the British government which kept the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians loyal to the British crown during the war in 1775 and in 1812.

s: British government strengthens French-Canadian nationalism (through generous measures)
q: It is certain, too, that these generous measures strengthened the position of the French race in Canada, made Canadians more jealous of their national identity, and led them to press for still wider liberties.

s: French-Canadian nationalism is defended by French Canadians (with demands for wider liberties)
q: these generous measures strengthened the position of the French race in Canada, made Canadians more jealous of their national identity, and led them to press for still wider liberties.

s: legislature of Lower Canada is a legislative body (first called in 1792)
q: This disposition became immediately apparent with the calling of the first parliament of Lower Canada in 1792.

s: Capitulation of Montreal assures French Canadians (property and civil rights)
q: The terms of the Capitulation of Montreal in 1760 assured the Canadians of their property and civil rights, and guaranteed to them 'the free exercise of their religion.'

s: French language is used in Assembly of Lower Canada (as a medium of debate and in official records and publications)
q: The outcome of the debate, as might have been expected, was to place the French language on a level with the English language in the records and publications of the Assembly, and French became, to all intents and purposes, the language of debate.

s: English language is used in Assembly of Lower Canada (alongside French in records and publications)
q: The outcome of the debate, as might have been expected, was to place the French language on a level with the English language in the records and publications of the Assembly

s: official recognition of French is a language policy (placing French on a level with English in Assembly records and publications)
q: The outcome of the debate, as might have been expected, was to place the French language on a level with the English language in the records and publications of the Assembly

s: French political majority in Lower Canada has majority in Assembly of Lower Canada (thirty-four members to sixteen)
q: The French-Canadian members, being in a majority of thirty-four to sixteen

s: English members of the Assembly owe election to French Canadians (all sixteen members represented in the Assembly)
q: And it should not be forgotten that all the sixteen English members, out of the fifty composing the Assembly, owed their election to French-Canadian voters.

s: racial bitterness in Lower Canada begins under Sir James Craig (later regime)
q: It was not until the regime of Sir James Craig that racial bitterness really began.

s: racial bitterness in Lower Canada is absent from Assembly of Lower Canada (during the early debates)
q: It must not be imagined, however, that in these early debates there was any of that rancour and animosity which later characterized the proceedings of the Assembly of Lower Canada.

s: Capitulation of Montreal guarantees French Canadians (free exercise of religion)
q: The terms of the Capitulation of Montreal in 1760 assured the Canadians of their property and civil rights, and guaranteed to them 'the free exercise of their religion.'

s: Quebec Act of 1774 grants French civil law (to the almost complete exclusion of English common law)
q: The Quebec Act of 1774 granted them the whole of the French civil law, to the almost complete exclusion of the English common law

s: Quebec Act of 1774 establishes French-Canadian Church (in Canada through legal enforcement of Catholic tithes)
q: and virtually established in Canada the Church of the vanquished through legal enforcement of the obligation resting upon Catholics to pay tithes.

s: Upper Canada is a province (created in 1791 and predominantly English)
q: when it became necessary in 1791 to divide Canada into two provinces, Upper Canada and Lower Canada, one predominantly English and the other predominantly French

s: Lower Canada is a province (created in 1791 and predominantly French)
q: when it became necessary in 1791 to divide Canada into two provinces, Upper Canada and Lower Canada, one predominantly English and the other predominantly French

s: Act of 1791 grants Upper Canada (political rights equal to those of Lower Canada)
q: the two provinces were granted precisely equal political rights.

s: Act of 1791 grants Lower Canada (political rights equal to those of Upper Canada)
q: the two provinces were granted precisely equal political rights.

s: French Canadians opposes The English proposal
q: The English proposal was opposed by the French

s: English population in Canada opposes the French proposal
q: the French proposal was opposed by the English

s: French Canadians dominate English population in Canada (politically in the province)
q: they declared that an end must be put to French-Canadian domination over English Canadians.

s: English population in Canada seek to oppose French Canadians (and their influence in the province)
q: Whether we be in peace or at war, it is essential {15} that we should make every effort, by every means available, to oppose the growth of the French and their influence

s: Sir James Craig is a governor of Canada
q: Sir James Craig, who became governor of Canada in 1807

s: Sir James Craig is a distinguished soldier
q: Sir James Craig, who became governor of Canada in 1807, was a distinguished soldier.

s: Sir James Craig has military service in South Africa
q: He had seen service in the American Revolutionary {16} War, in South Africa, and in India

s: Sir James Craig has military service in India
q: He had seen service in the American Revolutionary {16} War, in South Africa, and in India

s: Sir James Craig is inexperienced in civil government
q: He was, however, inexperienced in civil government and apt to carry his ideas of military discipline into the conduct of civil affairs.

s: Assembly of Lower Canada has majority French Canadians (in the House of Assembly)
q: As usual, the French-Canadian majority carried their point.

s: Sir James Craig is prejudiced against French Canadians
q: Moreover, he was prejudiced against the inhabitants and had doubts of their loyalty.

s: Sir James Craig is advised by Herman W. Ryland (as governor's secretary)
q: In Canada he surrounded himself with such men as Herman W. Ryland, the governor's secretary, and John Sewell, the attorney-general

s: Sir James Craig is advised by John Sewell (as attorney-general)
q: In Canada he surrounded himself with such men as Herman W. Ryland, the governor's secretary, and John Sewell, the attorney-general

s: John Sewell seeks to convert Canada (into an English colony)
q: The Province must be converted into an English Colony,' declared Sewell, 'or it will ultimately be lost to England.'

s: Sir James Craig dismisses five officers (in the summer of 1808)
q: In the summer of 1808 he dismissed from the militia five officers who were reputed to have a connection with that newspaper

s: Pierre Bedard is a member of the House of Assembly
q: but the conspicuous figure on the staff was Pierre Bedard, one of the members of the House of Assembly.

s: Pierre Bedard is a excellent mathematician
q: Bedard was an excellent mathematician, and was in the habit of whiling away the hours of his imprisonment by solving mathematical problems.

s: Sir George Prevost succeeds Sir James Craig (as governor of Canada)
q: It is {20} significant, too, that Craig's successor, Sir George Prevost, completely reversed his policy

s: racial bitterness in Lower Canada is a serious conflict (between French Canadians and English Canadians)
q: Yet out of the debate on this subject sprang the most serious racial conflict which had yet occurred in the province.

s: Sir George Prevost conciliates French Canadians (as governor)
q: He laid himself out to conciliate the French Canadians in every way possible

s: Sir George Prevost reverses Reign of Terror (by reversing Craig's policy)
q: Craig's successor, Sir George Prevost, completely reversed his policy.

s: War of 1812 reveals French-Canadian loyalty (in Lower Canada)
q: when the War of 1812 broke out, there proved to be less disloyalty in Lower Canada than in Upper Canada.

s: French-Canadian loyalty is greater in Lower Canada (than in Upper Canada during the War of 1812)
q: there proved to be less disloyalty in Lower Canada than in Upper Canada.

s: Lower Canada has less disloyalty (than Upper Canada during the War of 1812)
q: there proved to be less disloyalty in Lower Canada than in Upper Canada.

s: Upper Canada has more disloyalty (than Lower Canada during the War of 1812)
q: there proved to be less disloyalty in Lower Canada than in Upper Canada.

s: Bureaucrats surround Sir James Craig (during his administration)
q: Moreover, the blame for Craig's action during this period must be partly borne by the 'Bureaucrats' who surrounded him.

s: Bureaucrats seek to precipitate a disturbance (in order that the constitution of Lower Canada might be suspended)
q: there is at least a presumption, that some of these men actually wished to precipitate a disturbance, in order that the constitution of Lower Canada might be suspended and a new order of things inaugurated.

s: habeas corpus proceedings concern Pierre Bedard (after his arrest)
q: Soon after Bedard's arrest his friends applied for a writ of habeas corpus

s: English members of the Assembly levy direct tax on land
q: One, advocated by the English members, was to levy a direct tax on land

s: French political majority in Lower Canada impose extra customs duties
q: the other, proposed by the French members, was to impose extra customs duties.

s: French Canadians have interests agrarian (in the main)
q: for the simple reason that the interests of the French were in the main agrarian

s: English population in Canada have interests commercial (on the whole)
q: because the interests of the English were on the whole commercial.

s: Papineau is a born leader of men
q: His name was Louis Joseph Papineau. He was at that time only twenty-six years of age, but already his tall, well-built form, his fine features and commanding presence, marked him out as a born leader of men.

s: Assembly of Lower Canada lacks control of government (because the governor and Executive Council answer to the Colonial Office)
q: and in the second place, they had no control of the government, for the governor and his Executive Council were appointed by and responsible to the Colonial Office alone.

s: Assembly of Lower Canada lacks control of revenue (before the 1818 concession)
q: In Lower Canada, however, such a remedy was at first impossible, for the simple reason that the House of Assembly did not vote all the supplies necessary for carrying on the government.

s: Assembly of Lower Canada passes resolution about civil expenses (claiming ability and willingness to fund them)
q: In 1810, it is true, the Assembly had passed a resolution avowing its ability and willingness to vote 'the necessary sums for defraying the Civil Expenses of the Government of the Province.'

s: Assembly of Lower Canada receives control of revenue (apart from Crown dues and certain Imperial duties)
q: Through Sherbrooke's instrumentality the British government now decided to allow the Lower-Canadian legislature to vote the entire revenue of the province, apart from the casual and territorial dues of the Crown and certain duties levied by Act of the Imperial parliament.

s: Assembly of Lower Canada votes civil list (annually rather than for the sovereign's lifetime)
q: Unfortunately, however, the Assembly did not fall in with this view. It insisted, instead, on treating the civil list as an annual affair, and voting the salaries of the officials, from the governor {25} downwards, for only one year

s: Lower Canada is governed by Bureaucrats (through the governor and councils)

s: Bureaucrats is a local oligarchy (also known as the Chateau Clique)

s: Chateau Clique holds reins of government (in Lower Canada)
q: The members of the two councils were in the main of English birth, and they constituted a local oligarchy--known as the 'Bureaucrats' or the 'Chateau Clique'--which {23} held the reins of government

s: Legislative Council is composed mainly of English population in Canada (by birth)
q: The members of the two councils were in the main of English birth

s: Papineau holds seat in Assembly of Lower Canada (as a member)

s: British constitution provides control of the purse (through the House of Commons)
q: In England the remedy for a similar state of affairs had been found to lie in the control of the purse exercised by the House of Commons.

s: control of the purse is exercised by House of Commons (to compel the Executive through supply control)
q: In order to bring the Executive to its will, it was only necessary for that House to threaten the withholding of supplies.

s: British government accepts House of Assembly for Lower Canada revenue offer (during Sherbrooke's administration)
q: Later, however, in 1818, during the administration of Sir John Coape Sherbrooke, the offer of the Assembly was accepted by the Imperial government.

s: civil list is proposed as permanent funding (for the lifetime of the sovereign)
q: Sherbrooke's intention was that the legislature should vote out of this revenue a permanent civil list to be continued during the lifetime of the sovereign.

s: responsible government is advanced by Sir John Coape Sherbrooke (through constitutional recommendations)
q: he also recommended that the speaker of the House of Assembly should be included in the Council--a recommendation which was a preliminary move in the direction of responsible government.

s: Union Bill of 1822 threatens French Canadians (by subordinating the French to the English element)
q: There is little doubt that the real objects of the bill was the extinction of the Lower-Canadian Assembly and the subordination of the French to the English element in the colony. At any rate, the French Canadians saw in the bill a menace to their national existence.

s: John Neilson opposes Union Bill of 1822 (as an agent in London with Papineau)
q: Two agents were promptly appointed to go over to London to oppose it. One of them was Papineau; the other was John Neilson, the capable Scottish editor of the Quebec

s: John Neilson is editor of Quebec (Scottish)
q: the other was John Neilson, the capable Scottish editor of the Quebec

s: Lord Dalhousie is governor of Canada (in 1819)
q: Dalhousie, who had become governor of Canada in 1819.

s: Lord Dalhousie refuses to recognize Papineau (as speaker of the Assembly)
q: Consequently, when Papineau was elected to the speakership of the Assembly in 1827, Dalhousie refused to recognize him as speaker

s: Papineau is elected speaker of Assembly of Lower Canada (after the resignation of J. A. Panet)
q: In the Assembly his rise to prominence was meteoric; only three years after his entrance he was elected speaker on the resignation of the veteran {22} J. A. Panet, who had held the office at different times since 1792

s: Lord Goderich proposes civil list (in exchange for legislative control of provincial revenue)
q: Lord Goderich, who was at that time at the Colonial Office, instructed Lord Aylmer, who had become governor of Canada in 1830, to resign to the Assembly the control of the entire revenue of the province, with the single exception of the casual and territorial revenue of the Crown, if the Assembly would grant {30} in exchange a civil list of L19,000, voted for the lifetime of the king

s: Assembly of Lower Canada rejects Lord Goderich proposal (in the session of 1831)
q: But Papineau and his friends determined not to yield an inch of ground; and in the session of 1831 they succeeded in defeating the motion for the adoption of Lord Goderich's proposal.

s: French Canadians is regarded as members of an inferior race
q: They were regarded as members of an inferior race.

s: financial quarrel results in deadlock (between the Assembly and the Executive)
q: Thus commenced a struggle which was destined to last for many years. The Assembly refused to see that its action was really an encroachment upon the sphere of the Executive; and the Executive refused to place itself at the mercy of the Assembly. The result was deadlock.

s: Papineau possesses eloquence (according to his contemporaries)
q: He possessed an eloquence which, commonplace as it now appears on the printed page, apparently exerted a profound influence upon his contemporaries.

s: Papineau moves with French Canadians (rather than leading them, according to Christie)
q: It was indeed one of his characteristics, as the historian Christie has pointed out, that he seemed always 'to move with the masses rather than to lead them.'

s: Papineau opposes government (during the budget struggles)
q: But in the struggles over the budget he took up ground {26} strongly opposed to the government; and, when the question became acute, he threw restraint to the winds, and played the part of a dangerous agitator

s: Papineau declines seat on Executive Council (despite complaining that French Canadians lacked executive representation)
q: He complained that the French Canadians had no voice in the executive government, and that all the government offices were given to the English; yet when he was offered a seat in the Executive Council in 1822 he declined it

s: Assembly of Lower Canada has members The French-Canadian members of the Assembly
q: The French-Canadian members of the Assembly, having taken great pains to acquaint themselves with the law and custom of the British constitution, had awakened to the fact that they were not enjoying the position or the power which the members of the House of Commons in England were enjoying.

s: racial bitterness in Lower Canada grows in intensity
q: After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.

s: Papineau uses Assembly of Lower Canada (to expel or imprison opponents)
q: He did not scruple to use his majority either to expel from the House or to imprison those who incurred his wrath.

s: Papineau opposes bill for the independence of judges (after colonial-secretary amendments were accepted)
q: Quesnel had accepted some amendments suggested by the colonial secretary. This awoke the wrath of Papineau, who assailed the bill in his usual vehement style, and concluded by threatening Quesnel with the loss of his seat.

s: British constitution is regarded as bad (by Papineau by 1832)
q: By 1832 Papineau's political views had taken a more revolutionary turn. From being an admirer of the constitution of 1791, he had come to regard it as 'bad; very, very bad.'

s: elective Legislative Council seeks to change Legislative Council (from nominated to elective)
q: The chief change in the constitution which they proposed was the application of the elective principle to the Legislative Council.

s: Legislative Council is a nominated and reactionary legislative body (serving as a buffer)
q: The existing nominated and reactionary Legislative Council had served the purpose of a buffer between the governor's Executive Council and the Assembly.

s: Legislative Council buffers Executive Council (between the governor and the Assembly)
q: The existing nominated and reactionary Legislative Council had served the purpose of a buffer between the governor's Executive Council and the Assembly.

s: John Neilson supports Papineau (during the Dalhousie regime but not later)
q: Neilson, who had gone to England with him in 1822 and with Cuvillier and Viger in 1828, and who had supported him heartily during the Dalhousie regime, Papineau could no longer count.

s: Augustin Cuvillier follows John Neilson (in breaking with Papineau)
q: Augustin Cuvillier followed the lead of his friend Neilson, and so also did Andrew Stuart, one of the ablest lawyers in the province, and Quesnel.

s: Andrew Stuart follows John Neilson (in breaking with Papineau)
q: Augustin Cuvillier followed the lead of his friend Neilson, and so also did Andrew Stuart, one of the ablest lawyers in the province, and Quesnel.

s: Patriote party includes Louis Hippolyte LaFontaine (among Papineau's younger followers in the House)

s: Patriote party includes Augustin Norbert Morin (among Papineau's younger followers in the House)
q: Among his followers in the House were Louis Hippolyte LaFontaine, destined to become, ten years later, the colleague of Robert Baldwin in the LaFontaine-Baldwin administration, and Augustin Norbert Morin, the colleague of Francis Hincks in the Hincks-Morin administration of 1851.

s: Patriote party includes Wolfred Nelson (among English-speaking supporters)

s: Ninety-Two Resolutions is inspired by Papineau (although introduced by Elzear Bedard)

s: Ninety-Two Resolutions passes with fifty-six to twenty-four (in the Assembly of Lower Canada)
q: The Ninety-Two Resolutions secured a majority of fifty-six to twenty-four.

s: 1832 Montreal riot occurs in Montreal (during the west-ward by-election)
q: In 1832 a by-election in the west ward of Montreal culminated in a riot.

s: Ninety-Two Resolutions criticizes Legislative Council (for subservience to the Executive Council)
q: The subservience of the Legislative Council to the Executive Council; the partisanship of some of the judges; the maladministration of the wild lands; grave irregularities in the receiver-general's office; the concentration of a variety of public offices in the same persons; the failure of the governor to issue a writ for the election of a representative for the county of Montreal; and the expenditure of public moneys without the consent of the Assembly--all these, and many others, were enlarged upon.

s: Ninety-Two Resolutions demands impeachment of Lord Aylmer (in addition to his removal)
q: And when the Resolutions went on to demand, not merely the removal, but the impeachment of the governor, Lord Aylmer, it must have seemed to unprejudiced bystanders as if the framers of the Resolutions had taken leave of their senses.

s: Ninety-Two Resolutions supports elective Legislative Council (as its chief constitutional change)
q: The chief change in the constitution which they proposed was the application of the elective principle to the Legislative Council.

s: responsible government is a provincial cabinet system responsible to the legislature (with the governor bound to accept its advice on provincial affairs)

s: Papineau hastens responsible government (as an unwitting agent)

s: Catholic clergy withdraw from Papineau (because of his republican and revolutionary ideas)

s: French Canadians constitute the three killed and two wounded in the 1832 Montreal riot
q: After showing some forbearance under a fusillade of stones, they fired into the rioters, killing three and wounding two men, all of them French Canadians.

s: Papineau compares Lord Aylmer (unfavorably with Craig regarding repression)

s: Papineau has a large and powerful following (especially among the younger members)
q: Papineau still had, however, a large and powerful following, especially among the younger members.

s: Papineau is more and more violent and domineering (in the House)
q: In the House Papineau became more and more violent and domineering.

l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
s: The British conquest of Canada in the Seven Years' War placed French inhabitants under British rule, but the two communities generally lived together peacefully. French Canadians largely remained loyal to Great Britain during the American Revolution and the American invasion of Canada in 1775, encouraged by the policies of Murray and Carleton and the Quebec Act. They also fought alongside English Canadians during the War of 1812–1814, including Major de Salaberry's victory at Chateauguay. The later Rebellion in Canada was the only significant armed conflict between the two groups, with fighting at St Denis, St Charles, and St Eustache.

s: Canada came under British rule after the conquest in the Seven Years' War. French and English Canadians generally lived together in peace for a hundred and fifty years, apart from the Rebellion in Canada.

l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
s: The French inhabitants were placed under the rule of a people with a different language, religion, laws, temperament, and political outlook. Most remained in Canada after the conquest and generally lived peacefully with English Canadians.

s: English Canadians generally lived peacefully with French Canadians after the conquest. During the War of 1812–1814, they fought alongside French-Canadian militiamen, but during the Rebellion in Canada the two groups were arrayed against each other.

s: Canadians, whether English or French, have reason to view the record of relations between the two communities with satisfaction. The text describes a hundred and fifty years of general peace and amity, interrupted by only one limited and brief outbreak resembling civil war.

s: British rule in Canada began after the conquest in the Seven Years' War. The text examines how French Canadians generally remained loyal to the British crown under that rule, despite the later Rebellion in Canada.

s: The Seven Years' War ended with the conquest of Canada by British arms. This conquest placed the French inhabitants under British rule.

s: The conquest of Canada created the possibility of prolonged conflict between French inhabitants and the British conquerors. Instead, most French inhabitants stayed, and relations between French and English Canadians were generally peaceful.

s: Carleton was one of the successive governors whose conciliatory policy helped win the loyalty of French Canadians. When American forces invaded Canada in 1775, a much larger number of habitants enlisted under Carleton than joined the invaders.

s: The Quebec Act, passed in the year before the American invasion of Canada in 1775, granted concessions that helped produce French-Canadian loyalty to Great Britain.

s: During the American Revolution, efforts were made to persuade French Canadians to join the American cause. Most French Canadians resisted those appeals and remained at least passively loyal to Great Britain.

s: The Continental Congress sought to induce the French Canadians to join hands with the American revolutionaries. Its emissaries Franklin, Chase, and Carroll made eloquent appeals, but the mass of the people resisted them.

s: During the American invasion of Canada in 1775, Arnold and Montgomery invaded the colony. Most habitants remained at least passively loyal, while a few hundred may have joined the invaders and a much larger number enlisted under Carleton.

s: Quebec was besieged by Arnold during the American invasion of Canada in 1775. Canadian officers including Dupre, Dambourges, Dumas, and Marcoux helped Carleton drive back the invading Americans.

s: The French Revolution widened the separation between France and Canada. Its anti-clerical and republican tendencies had little in common with Canada, which was described as a child of the ancien regime.

s: During the War of 1812–1814, Canada was repeatedly invaded by American armies. French-Canadian militiamen under French-Canadian officers fought alongside English-speaking Canadians, and French-Canadian forces helped win the engagement at Chateauguay.

s: The United States invaded Canada during the War of 1812–1814. Its earlier revolutionary forces also invaded Canada in 1775, but French Canadians generally resisted joining them.

s: The Rebellion in Canada was the only occasion described as resembling civil war between French and English Canadians during a hundred and fifty years of British rule. l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The British granted the French inhabitants of Canada property, civil, religious, and political protections after the conquest, including French civil law and equal political rights in Upper Canada and Lower Canada. These concessions helped preserve French Canadian loyalty to the British crown while strengthening French national identity and demands for wider liberties. In the first Parliament of Lower Canada, French-speaking members secured the use of the French language alongside English in the Assembly's proceedings and publications. Early debates remained generally civil, although racial bitterness emerged later during the regime of Sir James Craig.

l: British, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The British protected the property and civil rights of the French inhabitants of Canada rather than treating them as a conquered people. They also granted religious and political concessions that helped maintain French Canadian loyalty.

l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The French inhabitants of Canada received guarantees of property, civil rights, and free religious exercise. They remained loyal to the British crown during the wars of 1775 and 1812, while becoming more jealous of their national identity and pressing for wider liberties.

l: Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: Canada received constitutional arrangements that preserved French civil law, recognized Catholic religious obligations, and divided the territory into Upper Canada and Lower Canada in 1791. French and English were subsequently used in the political proceedings of Lower Canada.

l: Capitulation of Montreal, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The Capitulation of Montreal in 1760 assured the Canadians of their property and civil rights and guaranteed them the free exercise of their religion.

l: Quebec Act of 1774, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The Quebec Act of 1774 granted the French civil law almost complete exclusion of the English common law. It also virtually established the Church of the vanquished through legal enforcement of Catholics' obligation to pay tithes.

l: French civil law, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The Quebec Act of 1774 restored the French civil law in Canada, making it the dominant legal system over the English common law.

s: The Roman Catholic Church was virtually established in Canada through the Quebec Act of 1774, which legally enforced the obligation of Catholics to pay tithes.

l: British government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The British government pursued a conciliatory policy toward the French inhabitants of Canada. It made no objection to the use of French in the law-courts and its concessions helped keep French Canadians loyal to the British crown.

l: British crown, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: The British crown retained the loyalty of the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians through conciliatory measures during the wars of 1775 and 1812.

l: Upper Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
s: Upper Canada was created in 1791 as one of two provinces, predominantly English in population. It received political rights equal to those of Lower Canada.
